titulo.texto: The War of 1847 and the Defense of the Capital

frase_gancho.texto: In eighteen forty-seven a foreign army reached the capital, and the decisive battle was fought on this very hill.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue to the next stop on the tour: another foreign intervention takes you to Puebla, to May fifth, eighteen sixty-two, and to the Orozco mural.

guion_corto.texto: Before eighteen forty-seven, Mexico had already faced Spanish attempts at reconquest and the Pastry War with France. Between eighteen forty-six and eighteen forty-eight, Mexico and the United States were at war. The American army advanced all the way to the Valley of Mexico. On August twentieth, eighteen forty-seven, fighting broke out at Churubusco. On September twelfth and thirteenth, the battle was fought in this castle, then home to the Military College. When Chapultepec fell, the troops of General Winfield Scott occupied the capital. On February second, eighteen forty-eight, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo set the Rio Grande as the border. Mexico ceded Upper California and New Mexico. The museum devotes a hall to the Battle of Chapultepec and remembers the civilians and soldiers who died defending the country.

guion_largo.texto:
The war of eighteen forty-seven was not the first conflict with a foreign power. In eighteen twenty-nine, a Spanish army under Isidro Barradas tried to reconquer Mexico and surrendered in Tamaulipas, decimated by fevers. In eighteen thirty-eight, France blockaded Veracruz and demanded six hundred thousand pesos, among them sixty thousand claimed by a French pastry cook from Tacubaya. That is why it is called the Pastry War. In that war, a cannon shot cost Santa Anna his left leg. In the Texan Secession Hall, dedicated to eighteen thirty-six, the museum displays a flag taken at the Alamo from the Gray Volunteers, American mercenaries.

The United States Congress declared war on Mexico in eighteen forty-six. It ended with a treaty in eighteen forty-eight. This hill was the last great stage of a campaign that reached the Valley of Mexico.

On August twentieth, eighteen forty-seven, fighting broke out at the former convent of Churubusco. About six thousand American soldiers fired on the improvised fortress, and the defense lasted some two and a half hours. The Mexicans fought until they ran out of ammunition, which was then known by an older name. When General David Twiggs demanded their weapons, General Pedro María Anaya answered with a phrase that is remembered every August twentieth: if there were ammunition, you would not be here. The sources record it with small variations, such as: as if we had ammunition. According to the INAH, more than three hundred fifty Mexican soldiers died in that engagement.

At Churubusco the Saint Patrick's Battalion also fought, made up mostly of Irish immigrants who had deserted from the American army. The sources mention several reasons. They were Catholics and felt mistreated in an army with a Protestant majority. Historians add the brutal discipline and the offers of land and money from the Mexican side. John Riley organized the unit and made it a specialist in artillery. It is said that its flag bore Saint Patrick on one side, and a harp with the Mexican coat of arms on the other.

After the defeat, the Americans captured eighty-five Irishmen and charged seventy-two with desertion. Fifty were sentenced to the gallows. The other twenty-two received fifty lashes and a letter D branded on the cheek or the hip. Riley, the leader of the battalion, was punished with the whip and the brand, not with the gallows.

Between September tenth and thirteenth they were hanged at San Ángel and at Mixcoac. According to American historians, the condemned men at Mixcoac were placed where they could see Chapultepec. There they watched the Mexican flag come down and the American flag go up. The Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that General William Harney ordered the executions to coincide with that moment, and it speaks of thirty men.

On September twelfth, American artillery bombarded this castle, then home to the Military College, and on the thirteenth the main assault came. It was defended by General Nicolás Bravo with about a thousand soldiers and some fifty cadets. At the [terrace of the Child Heroes](chap_25_terraza_ninos_heroes), the young people who died are remembered. Bravo surrendered on September thirteenth at nine thirty in the morning, but the people of the capital kept fighting the American artillery for thirty-seven consecutive hours. On September fourteenth, American troops occupied Mexico City. The museum also holds a mural by Gabriel Flores, painted in nineteen seventy, about that assault.

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed on February second, eighteen forty-eight. It set the Rio Grande as the border. Mexico ceded Upper California and New Mexico, territories where California, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming now lie. That is about two million three hundred thousand square kilometers. The United States paid fifteen million dollars. American troops left the capital on June twelfth, after the Mexican Congress ratified the treaty on May twenty-fifth.

If you want to follow the trail of Churubusco and of the Saint Patrick's Battalion, the former convent now houses the National Museum of the Interventions. The nineteenth century would still bring another foreign intervention, the French one. At the next stop you will see how the Republic confronted it, with the [Battle of Puebla and the Orozco mural](chap_09_batalla_puebla_orozco).

texto.Conflict: War between Mexico and the United States, 1846-1848

texto.pregunta: Myth: Mexico voluntarily sold California and New Mexico.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The treaty was signed on February 2, 1848, with American troops quartered in the capital, and they did not leave until June 12. The United States paid 15 million dollars, but the cession came at the end of a lost war, not of a commercial negotiation. The only sale of territory was a different one, that of La Mesilla in 1853: about 76,845 km2 in exchange for 10 million dollars, in a region the United States wanted for a railroad.
